decision.detail: I walk the corridor from the booth to the station patch. The ballroom lights catch the glass of the reel canister as I turn the corner—amber, then a flash of blue, then nothing. The old projectionist is standing by the doorframe, hands in his cardigan pockets, watching me go. I stop. Let him have two seconds. He says something about the sprocket holes, how you can hear the film thinking. I nod. I don't turn the camera on. There's no tape left anyway. I keep walking. At the patch counter I set the canister down flat, label side up, and press my thumb on it for a second so it doesn't slide. Rita's already there, headset half on, talking low to whoever's on the line. She sees the reel. Doesn't look up yet. I tap the counter once with my knuckle. She slides the canister toward herself, pops the lid, checks the spool. Closes the lid. Nods. I pull my coat collar up. The station line hums under my feet, that low electrical thrum you feel through the soles of your boots. I leave. No handshake. No 'thanks, Larry.' The door clicks behind me into the February dark.
decision.intention: Alma's voice is on the patch now. Her daughter will hear it before the line closes for the night. The reel is Rita's problem after this—she'll feed it into the regional feed, Pittsburgh will get it by Thursday at the latest. My job tonight is done. One take. One voice. The lights in the ballroom are still on, still spectacular, and I can see them from the street, but I'm not going back in. I'm going to walk home through the cold and not think about the projectionist's face, or Phil's saucer, or the fact that I said 'be back for the party' and I don't know if there is a party. I'm going to walk home. The reel is where it needs to be. That's the whole job.
decision.words: I say nothing to the projectionist. Just the nod. At the counter, to Rita, not looking up from the canister: 'Last one. Sprocket's clean.' Then I'm out the door.
